title: Power
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — The Rate of Energy Delivery

Two cranes can lift the same car, but only the powerful one lifts it quickly. Power measures work per unit time — the billing unit of the electricity grid (the kilowatt-hour) and the performance metric of engines, pumps and athletes.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

| Quantity | Definition | Formula | Unit |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Power** | Work done per unit time | $P = W/t$ | watt (W) = J/s |
| **Instantaneous power** | Rate at an instant | $P = \vec F\cdot\vec v = Fv\cos\theta$ | W |
| **Kilowatt-hour** | Commercial energy unit: energy delivered by 1 kW for 1 hour | $1\,\text{kWh} = 3.6 \times 10^6$ J | — |

**NEB 2024 (2m):** 1 kWh = 1000 W × 3600 s = **$3.6 \times 10^6$ J** — the unit on every electricity bill.

### 2.1 Worked numericals

**Q1 (3m, 2022/2024):** An electric motor has a power output of 2 kW. How much time will it take to lift a 500 kg mass through 20 m? (g = 10 m/s²)
*Work needed:* $W = mgh = 500 \times 10 \times 20 = 10^5$ J.
*Time:* $t = W/P = 10^5/2000 = $ **50 s**.

**Q2 (3m, 2022):** A person of mass 60 kg climbs a staircase of vertical height 8 m in 20 s (g = 9.8). Calculate the power developed.
*Work:* $W = mgh = 60 \times 9.8 \times 8 = 4704$ J.
*Power:* $P = 4704/20 = $ **235.2 W** (about 0.24 kW — a healthy human output).

**Q3 (3m, 2024):** A car of mass 1000 kg moves at a uniform speed of 20 m/s against a total resistive force of 500 N. What power must the engine develop?
*Uniform speed → engine force equals resistance:* $F = 500$ N.
*Power:* $P = Fv = 500 \times 20 = $ **10,000 W = 10 kW.**

## 3. Conceptual Relationships

- **To Topic 16:** power is work's time derivative — same energy, different delivery rate.
- **To Topic 18:** $P = Fv$ comes from differentiating the work–energy theorem: $P = dW/dt = F\,ds/dt$.
- **To electrical circuits (Unit 25):** $P = VI = I^2R = V^2/R$ — the same watt in electrical dress.
- **To real life:** electricity bills (kWh), engine horsepower (1 hp ≈ 746 W) and human sprint outputs (~1 kW briefly) are all this topic.

### 4.3 Common examination mistakes

1. Forgetting $P = Fv$ for uniform-speed vehicles — the engine force equals the resistance, not $ma$.
2. Using g = 9.8 in one numerical and 10 in another inconsistently.
3. Confusing kWh (energy) with kW (power).
4. Ignoring the vertical height in staircase problems — only mgh counts.
5. Arithmetic slips with $3.6 \times 10^6$ J per kWh.

summary: Power is the rate of energy delivery: $P = W/t$, or instantaneously $P = \vec F\cdot\vec v$ — for a vehicle at uniform speed the engine force just balances resistance, so $P = F_{res}v$ (a 1000 kg car at 20 m/s against 500 N needs 10 kW — NEB 2024). Lifting numericals divide the work by the power: a 2 kW motor raises 500 kg through 20 m (10⁵ J) in 50 s (NEB 2022 & 2024); a 60 kg climber ascending 8 m in 20 s develops 235 W (NEB 2022). The commercial energy unit is the **kilowatt-hour**: 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J (NEB 2024). Power prices speed of delivery, not the size of the job.
specificConditions: P=F⃗·v⃗ uses instantaneous force and velocity; it applies even when force changes with time.
For efficiency, state whether the requested power is input or useful output.

notes: Power is the rate of energy transfer: average P=ΔW/Δt and instantaneous P=dW/dt. Its SI unit is watt, 1 W=1 J s⁻¹.
For translation, dW=F⃗·dr⃗ gives P=F⃗·v⃗=Fv cosθ. Only the force component parallel to velocity transfers energy; a perpendicular centripetal force does no work in uniform circular motion.

Worked example: a 200 kg load rises steadily at 0.50 m s⁻¹. The lifting force is mg=1960 N for g=9.8 m s⁻², so useful power is Fv=980 W. In 10 s the load rises 5 m and gains 9800 J, confirming P=W/t=980 W.
At constant speed, net power is zero because engine power balances resistive forces. For rotation, P=τ⃗·ω⃗; efficiency η=Pout/Pin distinguishes useful output from input.
A 50 N force at 60° to a crate moving at 3.0 m s⁻¹ transfers energy at P=50×3×cos60°=75 W, not 150 W.
